lesson.menu_title: The Art of the Executive Question
lesson.menu_desc: Asking, probing and redirecting in a case room -- 31 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- The Art of the Executive Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Marcio Ferreira Santos | Lesson 12 -- The Executive Question
phases: The Question You Did Not Ask

listenings.text: Good morning. Before we open the case, one house rule. In this room, the person who asks the sharpest question learns more than the person who gives the longest answer, so I want questions early and I want them specific. If a number in the exhibit does not make sense to you, say so. The odds are that thirty other people are quiet for exactly the same reason. And when you push on something, push on the premise, not on the person. I would want to probe the assumption behind exhibit four is a serious question. The author is wrong is a comment, and comments end conversations. One more thing. If you need clarification, ask for it in the first ten minutes, not in the last five. That is everything. Let us open the case.

Can I give you the note from the mock interview? Your content was strong. The pricing story landed. But when I asked you where the limits of your model are, you answered in two seconds, and that speed reads as defensive, not confident. Here is what a senior candidate does instead. First, buy yourself the room. That is an important question. Before I answer directly, let me give you some context. Then, and this is the part almost nobody does, ask something back. Could I ask what kind of limit you have in mind, technical or commercial? You are not stalling. You are making sure you answer the question they actually asked, and you sound like a peer instead of a candidate. Try it again on Thursday. Same question, and take four seconds before you speak.

extra_audio.text: First, the interviewer asks a wide and difficult question. Then the candidate buys the room with a short redirect line. After that, he asks an indirect question to find out what the interviewer really means. Next, he answers the narrower question with one example. Finally, he checks that the answer landed with a tag question.

reading.rtitle: Session 4 — Pre-Read: How the Case Discussion Works
paras: Welcome to Session 4. Before Thursday, read the case and prepare three questions. Not three comments. Three questions. In a case discussion the fastest way to be heard is to probe an assumption that everyone else in the room has accepted in silence.

A strong question does one of four things. It seeks clarification: just to make sure I am reading the exhibit correctly, is that figure gross or net? It asks for elaboration: I would be curious to understand how you arrived at that range. It tests a premise: if we accept the premise that volume drives price, what happens in a category where it does not? Or it draws out an implication that the author left unsaid.

Watch your qualifiers. Prices always fall when a competitor enters is an assertion. Prices usually fall in the first two quarters when a competitor enters at scale is an argument. The second one survives the room, because the nuance is built into the sentence.

One last note on tone. Participants often think that a hard question is an aggressive one. It is not. That is an interesting result, isn't it? opens a door. Your number is wrong closes it. You are here to think out loud with sixty other people, and nobody does that well in a room where questions feel like attacks.
reading.source: Program note, executive education (adapted for class)

gist.prompt: Read once for the main idea. What does this note ask participants to prepare?
choices: Three comments defending their own company's strategy
Three questions that probe, clarify or test the case
A written summary of every exhibit in the case

items: The note asks for three questions rather than three comments.
The first paragraph says it directly: not three comments, three questions.
Asking for elaboration is one of the four things a strong question does.
The second paragraph lists clarification, elaboration, testing a premise and drawing out an implication.
The note calls "prices always fall when a competitor enters" a well-built argument.
It calls that sentence an assertion. The version with qualifiers is the argument.
According to the note, a hard question and an aggressive question are the same thing.
The last paragraph says the opposite: a hard question is not an aggressive one.
